segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came to Jesus by night and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born from above, they cannot see the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nicodemus said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How can a person be born when he is an old man? He cannot enter his mother’s womb a second time and be born, can he?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born of water and Spirit, they cannot enter the kingdom of God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not be amazed that I said to you, ‘You must all be born from above.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nicodemus answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How can these things happen?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You are the teacher of Israel, and you do not understand these things?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly, truly, I tell you, we speak of what we know and testify to what we have seen, yet you do not accept our testimony.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If I have told you about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God did not send the Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because they have not believed in the name of the one and only Son of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light, because their deeds were evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For everyone who practices what is base hates the light and does not come to the light, so that their deeds may not be exposed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be shown that their deeds have been done in God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and there he spent time with them and was baptizing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John too was baptizing, at Aenon near Salim, because there was plenty of water there, and people were coming and being baptized;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for John had not yet been thrown into prison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then a dispute arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew about purification.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to John and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, the one who was with you across the Jordan, the one you have testified about—look, he is baptizing, and everyone is going to him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “A person cannot receive even one thing unless it has been given to him from heaven.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You yourselves testify for me that I said, ‘I am not the Messiah,’ but, ‘I have been sent ahead of him.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. But the bridegroom’s friend, who stands and listens to him, is overjoyed at the bridegroom’s voice. So this joy of mine is now complete.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He must increase, but I must decrease.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who comes from above is above all. The one who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth. The one who comes from heaven is above all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He testifies to what he has seen and heard, yet no one accepts his testimony.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever has accepted his testimony has set their seal to this: God is true.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever disobeys the Son will not see life; instead, the wrath of God remains on them.

notes.note: The Greek adverb can mean either 'from above' or 'again', and the conversation turns on that double sense: Nicodemus hears 'a second time' (verse 4), while Jesus goes on to speak of birth from the Spirit. Elsewhere in John, including verse 31 of this chapter, the word means 'from above', so that sense is given in the text. Many translations keep 'born again' and footnote the alternative; scholars widely agree that both meanings are in play and that no single English word carries both.

notes.phrase: You must all be born from above
notes.note: Greek distinguishes singular and plural 'you'. Jesus addresses Nicodemus in the singular, but here he switches to the plural, and the 'you' in 'you do not accept' (verse 11) and throughout verse 12 is plural as well. Nicodemus, who began with 'we know' in verse 2, is being addressed as the representative of a wider group.

notes.phrase: The wind blows where it wishes
notes.traditional: The wind blows where it wishes
notes.note: One Greek word means 'wind', 'breath' and 'spirit', and the word translated 'sound' also means 'voice'. The sentence can therefore also be heard as 'The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice'; the comparison works in Greek because the same word serves for both. Like most translations, this one gives 'wind' here and 'Spirit' at the end of the verse.

The reference is to Numbers 21:4-9, where Moses set a bronze snake on a pole and those bitten by snakes lived when they looked at it. The Greek verb means both to raise something physically and to exalt. John uses it of Jesus being raised on the cross (see 12:32-33), and most interpreters think the sense of exaltation is intended as well.

The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage of the period 'eternal life' meant the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. In John this life is spoken of as something the believer already has (see verse 36).

notes.phrase: may have eternal life in him
notes.traditional: whoever believes in him may have eternal life
notes.note: The words 'in him' can be taken with 'believes' or with 'have eternal life'. John's regular expression for believing in someone uses a different preposition, as in verse 16, which favours the second reading adopted here. Many translations take the first, and some manuscripts have John's usual preposition, with a number also adding 'may not perish' from verse 16.

notes.phrase: For God so loved the world
notes.note: Ancient manuscripts have no quotation marks, and it is unclear where Jesus's words to Nicodemus end. This translation closes the speech at verse 15 and treats verses 16-21 as the evangelist's own reflection, because of the shift to past tenses and to phrasing that elsewhere belongs to the narrator. Many translations and red-letter editions continue Jesus's speech through verse 21, and scholars are divided.

The Greek adverb normally means 'in this way', but paired with the following 'that' it can also express degree, 'so much'. The traditional 'so loved' is kept because, like the Greek, it can be heard either way. Some scholars argue for 'this is how God loved the world: he gave', while the majority of translations understand 'loved so much that he gave'.

The Greek word means 'the only one of its kind' and was used of an only child; its second half is related to 'kind', not to 'beget'. 'One and only' or 'only' is the usual modern rendering. A minority of scholars have recently defended the older 'only begotten'.

Most English translations have 'condemn' in verses 17 and 18 and then 'judgment' or 'verdict' in verse 19, though some keep 'judge' throughout. The Greek uses the ordinary verb for judging and its related noun across all three verses; the context shows that an adverse judgment is meant. 'Judge' is kept so that the connection is visible, both here and with later passages in John where judgment is discussed.

The Greek word translates the Hebrew for 'anointed one', the king Israel was expecting. Here John is denying a title, not using a name, so 'Messiah' is used; where the word functions as part of Jesus's name, this translation keeps 'Christ'. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

notes.phrase: The one who comes from above is above all
notes.note: It is unclear whether verses 31-36 continue John the Baptist's speech or are the evangelist's comment. They are treated here as the evangelist's words, since they echo the language of the conversation with Nicodemus and of verses 16-21. Some translations keep the quotation open to the end of the chapter, and the question is disputed.

notes.phrase: he gives the Spirit without measure
notes.traditional: God gives the Spirit without measure
notes.note: The Greek does not state the subject of 'gives'. Most interpreters understand that God gives the Spirit without limit to the one he has sent, and some manuscripts add 'God' to make this explicit. It is also possible to read it as the one sent giving the Spirit without limit; the translation leaves 'he' as open as the Greek.

candidates.reason: Means both 'from above' and 'again/from the beginning'; it recurs in John 3:31, 19:11, James and elsewhere, and John 3:3, 7 needs a fixed policy on the wordplay.
Translations alternate between 'judge' and 'condemn' for the same verb, obscuring links with κρίσις and with judgment passages across John, Paul and the Synoptics.
Jesus's formula 'Amen (amen) I say to you' occurs throughout the Gospels and is rendered variously as 'truly', 'verily', 'amen', 'I assure you'; it needs one rendering.
A key term in John, Acts and Revelation with its noun μαρτυρία; translators vary between 'testify', 'bear witness' and 'witness', and the verb-noun link should stay visible.
Covers wind, breath, human spirit and the Holy Spirit, and the capitalisation decision (Spirit or spirit) is an interpretive choice that recurs across the whole New Testament.
